rv.q: "In one of Gold’s riskier directorial flourishes, the dead of 'Macbeth' never really leave. Even aside from the usual ghosts and apparitions, Gold’s stage will be populated by the sitting, silent victims of all that bloodletting, a choice that casts an appropriately spooky spell even as it – along with an unnecessary, weirdly upbeat visual coda ...
I was entertained, and heard some great language spoken by legends of my time.
It’s a production that makes you think, but it did not make me feel.
But this relentlessly analytical production, directed by Sam Gold, takes even that last quality apart, offering not so much “Macbeth” as a private inquest into it.
Yet, despite the charms and potions, there’s not so much magic here.
Gold’s production simply lacks narrative drive. You cannot get fully invested in an evening spent pondering Macbeth’s narrative psyche if you don’t comprehend the world.
Deliberately murky, this anemic modern-dress production creeps at a petty pace from scene to scene.
It’s a grizzly and unearned grasp for thrills from a production without a cohesive life force of its own.
Under all the fog (and there is a lot of it), there isn't much substance in this production, which clearly prioritizes an aesthetic and a mood over acting, coherence and Shakespeare's text.
Nevertheless, their talent cannot redeem this overwrought, underacted Skyfail.
In retrospect, that seems appropriate, since this is far more Sam Gold’s Macbeth than the Bard’s.
Misguided in execution and largely indifferently acted, this minimalist production does no favors to either of its talented stars.
This is not a grand Macbeth — the staging is too sparse and self-aware, almost tossed-off (or at least determined to give that impression), for that.
These opening and final vistas are not as written by Shakespeare, and the closing one in particular feels bizarre and hokey considering what has just preceded it.
In the end, this Macbeth is a star-enhanced hodgepodge.
Gold’s production underplays everyone’s emotions to the point of nothingness.
Whatever his rationale, Gold likes to bring a downtown, experimental theater perspective to Broadway, where, really, it simply does not work, at least not with this production of Macbeth.
Mr. Craig and Ms. Negga both offer clearly articulated but superficial performances.
This Macbeth hovers in a fog of confusion from beginning to end, which features the actors chowing down on soup as they stare out at the hungry and irritated crowd.
The much-anticipated Sam Gold–directed Broadway production of Macbeth, which just opened at the Longacre Theatre, appears to be a comedy.
The staging sometimes feels like an acting exercise conducted during a rehearsal.
Fine actors like Daniel Craig and Ruth Negga who have demonstrated their top-flight acting chops on stage elsewhere have not been aided by the bizarre direction.
Classic works don’t need the modern-dress approach that nowadays is a shabby cliché.
It’s an experience for all the senses from the moment you step into the theatre.
It was actually disconcerting and diminished the tragic elements of the play about a power-hungry man and the destruction his ambitions create.
I can't imagine what someone who's never seen or read the play could possibly get here, except an excuse to catch up on their sleep.

cn.t: Sam Gold's minimalist "Macbeth" starring Daniel Craig and Ruth Negga draws mostly negative reviews for its eccentric, self-indulgent staging that overshadows the leads, though the stars earn some praise when allowed to shine through the director's puzzling choices.
